newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea's corruption scandal nears a climax.
newsitem.headline: South Korea's corruption scandal nears a climax.

text.p: A corruption scandal that has rocked South Korea neared its climax on Friday as President Kim Young-sam's son admitted receiving several million dollars during a marathon grilling by state prosecutors.
But there were unconfirmed reports that Kim Hyun-chul, who has denied the money was in return for business favours, would fight to prove his innocence through the courts.
The arrest of the president's second son, nicknamed the "crown prince", now appears likely on Saturday.

Embattled President Kim Young-sam is expected to make an announcement on the scandal next week to try to limit the damage from an affair that has shredded his credibility and turned him into a lame duck during his final year in office.
"The president is expected to make his stand known on the current political situation sometime next week," a presidential Blue House official said.
Meanwhile, two of Kim Hyun-chul's business associates were indicted on fraud, bribery and other charges.
And a former security official accused of managing political slush funds for the younger Kim was brought in by state prosecutors for questioning.
Prosecutors said they had secured evidence that Kim Hyun-chul took at least three billion won ($3.4 million) from businessmen, several of them alumni of his high school.
The younger Kim was summoned on Thursday and grilled overnight. He must either be arrested or released by Saturday afternoon.
Yonhap Television News reported that Kim Hyun-chul told a friend before reporting to prosecutors that corruption charges against him were trumped up and he would take legal action to defend himself.
Any show of defiance by the younger Kim, who is reviled by many ordinary South Koreans and has been abandoned even by his father, would inevitably prolong a national crisis.
It would put further pressure on the president, who is anxious to put the affair behind him.

The two associates who were indicted, Park Tae-joong and Kim Hi-chan, were arrested this month after prosecutors accused them of taking bribes in return for promises to lobby Kim Hyun-chul for help obtaining broadcast licences.
Kim Ki-sup, the one-time deputy intelligence chief, is accused by opposition politicians of managing seven billion won in leftover funds from President Kim's 1992 election campaign.
The Joong-Ang Ilbo daily said the arrest of Kim Hyun-chul would deal a "fatal blow" to the moral standing of the Kim Young-sam administration.
"His arrest in a way serves as a judgement on the current administration," it said in an editorial.

The scandal erupted when the nation's second largest steelmaker, Hanbo Steel Co, collapsed in January under debts of five trillion won. The failure uncovered a web of corruption involving top bankers, tycoons and politicians.
Opposition parties have alleged that Hanbo received preferential loans as a reward for donations of up to 90 billion won to Kim Young-sam's election campaign.
They accuse Kim Hyun-chul, who helped engineer his father's election victory, of laundering unspent campaign funds through his business cronies.
Eleven people, including three top aides of President Kim, are standing trial over the Hanbo scandal.
Kim Young-sam was swept to power on an anti-graft ticket, and put his two immediate predecessors, Chun Doo Hwan and Roh Tae-woo, into jail on corruption and other charges.
President Kim has faced mounting pressure to fully account for his campaign financing. ($1 = 891 won)
